title: US Oil Reserve Hits 44-Year Low as Europe's Gas Storage Slips to 61.6% Ahead of Winter; Trump Sends Saudi Nuclear Deal to Congress
subhead: The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve fell to 298.7 million barrels — its lowest since 1982 — while Europe's gas storage sits at 61.6% full versus 74% a year ago, a twin strategic-reserve squeeze as the Iran conflict keeps Gulf supply offline. Separately, Trump sent the US-Saudi civil nuclear deal to Congress, and Iran and Oman floated a temporary Hormuz corridor.

sections.heading: Strategic Reserves Run Low on Both Sides of the Atlantic
sections.body:
The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve fell to 298.7 million barrels in the week ending August 21, its lowest level since November 1982, according to Department of Energy and EIA data cited by Telesur. The drawdown marks 20 consecutive weeks of decline since late March, during which authorities released 116.7 million barrels from the emergency stockpile to cushion the Hormuz disruption. The all-time low remains 288.1 million barrels from November 1982, meaning the reserve is now within roughly 10 million barrels of its historic floor.

Across the Atlantic, Europe faces a parallel squeeze. Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE) data cited by AzerNews shows European gas storage at 61.6% full, versus 74% at the same point last year, with TTF prices at the Netherlands hub reaching €68.36 per megawatt-hour. IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol warned Europe could face serious winter risks from Middle East supply disruptions and suspended Russian LNG, while Wood Mackenzie flagged historically low storage as a security-of-supply risk for winter 2026-27. The EU's target of 80% storage by December 1 looks increasingly out of reach.
sections.whyItMatters: Both the world's largest strategic oil reserve and Europe's gas buffer are being drawn down at the same time the Gulf's main export route stays shut. The US has far less cushion to absorb a fresh supply shock, and Europe enters winter with a thinner margin than it planned.

sections.heading: Iran and Oman Float a Temporary Hormuz Corridor
sections.body:
Iran said it had restarted talks with Oman on managing the Strait of Hormuz, with the two countries discussing 'a joint temporary navigational corridor' and agreeing to clear the waterway of mines, Reuters reported. Trump repeated his claim that all mines in the strait had been cleared. But Iran's deputy foreign minister cautioned that 'the understanding between Iran and Oman does not mean the opening of the Strait of Hormuz', per ET Now. The strait, which handled roughly one-fifth of global oil and LNG shipments before the war began in February, remains largely shut.

The fragility of the corridor was underscored on Tuesday when an oil tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile and disabled about 9 nautical miles northeast of Oman's Ash Shishah, at the strait's entrance, the UK Maritime Trade Operations said. Oil markets nonetheless rallied on the diplomatic signal: Brent fell 2% to $86.80 a barrel and WTI dropped 1.8% to $80.87, a second straight day of declines on Hormuz reopening hopes, per Times Now.
sections.whyItMatters: A mine-cleared, jointly managed corridor would be the first concrete step toward restoring Gulf flows since February — but Tehran's insistence that it is not a full reopening, plus the fresh tanker strike, shows the route remains a live battlefield, not a settled trade lane.

sections.heading: US Sanctions Squeeze Bites as Iran's Shadow Fleet Gathers Off Sri Lanka
sections.body:
Washington is threatening to punish countries that continue doing business with Iran, though it said it would not impose penalties immediately, Reuters reported. Iran denounced the effort as an act of 'gross lawlessness' and expressed confidence many countries would not join the pressure campaign. The squeeze is visibly binding: ship-tracking data and a Financial Times report cited by Times Now show around 13 Iran-flagged tankers and several shadow-fleet vessels anchored just outside Sri Lanka's territorial waters, unable to return to Iran amid the US blockade.

The economic pressure is taking a political toll at home for Tehran. Reuters/Ipsos polling cited by CNBC-TV18 shows US public approval of the war at its lowest since the conflict's early days, with Trump's popularity at a record low ahead of November congressional elections. Iran's President Pezeshkian has publicly said 'war must come to an end,' per ET Now, an acknowledgment that the economic war is working.
sections.whyItMatters: The sanctions architecture is now visibly strangling Iran's shipping — tankers stranded offshore, unable to dock or return — even as Washington withholds immediate penalties to give diplomacy room. The question is whether Tehran's economic pain forces a Hormuz concession before the corridor talks collapse.

sections.heading: Trump Sends Saudi Nuclear Deal to Congress
sections.body:
President Trump sent the proposed US-Saudi civil nuclear agreement to Congress on Monday, a 30-year deal that would allow US companies to export civilian nuclear technology and build AP1000 reactors worth tens of billions of dollars, benefiting Westinghouse (jointly owned by Cameco and Brookfield), Reuters reported. The administration official said the pact will only take effect if Saudi Arabia joins the Abraham Accords and normalizes relations with Israel — a condition Riyadh has resisted, demanding an irreversible path to a Palestinian state first.

Congress has 90 session days to consider the deal; unless it objects, the agreement goes into force. Democratic lawmakers and nonproliferation advocates have criticized the pact for not barring Saudi enrichment or reprocessing — the 'gold standard' the UAE accepted in 2009. Henry Sokolski of the Nonproliferation Policy Education Center called the process 'hardly ideal if you're serious about no enrichment and recognition of Israel.'
sections.whyItMatters: Sending the deal to Congress starts a 90-day clock that could let it proceed even without the normalization and nonproliferation conditions Trump attached — a real risk of the US enabling Saudi enrichment while simultaneously bombing Iran over its nuclear program.

sections.heading: India Pivots to US for LPG and LNG as Gulf Disruption Bites
sections.body:
India has sharply increased purchases of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and LNG from the United States as West Asia conflict disrupts Gulf supplies, PTI reported. US LPG imports have surged to 73% of India's total, per Moneycontrol, a dramatic reorientation of a supply chain that historically leaned on Gulf producers. The shift strengthens India's energy security but comes at a cost — longer shipping routes and higher freight, analysts note.

Separately, Indian refiners are leaning on Russia, the UAE and South America for August crude imports amid the supply disruption, according to The Hindu BusinessLine, and analysts warn China's scramble for oil under US Iran sanctions could add to India's crude and freight costs.
sections.whyItMatters: India is quietly re-engineering its energy import map — away from the Gulf and toward the US and Russia — a structural shift that outlasts the current war and deepens New Delhi's energy ties with Washington even as it keeps buying Russian barrels.

sections.heading: SLB Wins Access to Venezuela's Oilfield Data
sections.body: US oil-services giant SLB signed a contract with Venezuela's PDVSA last week granting it access to the country's oilfield data — the world's largest crude reserves — three sources told Reuters. The deal lets SLB upgrade and organize PDVSA's outdated database, which has been neglected for years and damaged by a ransomware attack late last year. Venezuela has not published comprehensive oil statistics since 2015, a barrier to attracting investment. SLB will use technologies including artificial intelligence to modernize and restore the reliability of the data, with the aim of digitizing and consolidating the industry's records, one source said.
sections.whyItMatters: A US firm gaining privileged access to Venezuela's long-opaque oil data is a quiet but significant step toward reopening the country's reserves to outside investment — potentially adding heavy crude supply to a market starved by the Hormuz closure, though sanctions and PDVSA's dysfunction remain obstacles.

bottomLine: The defining development of the day is a twin strategic-reserve squeeze: the US SPR at a 44-year low and Europe's gas storage at 61.6% versus 74% a year ago, both drawn down while Hormuz stays largely shut. Iran and Oman floated a temporary navigational corridor and agreed to clear mines, but Tehran insists it is not a full reopening and a tanker was struck at the strait's entrance — so the diplomatic signal is real but fragile. Oil fell to $86.80 on the hopes. Meanwhile Trump sent the Saudi nuclear deal to Congress, starting a 90-day clock that could let it proceed without the normalization and nonproliferation conditions he attached, and India quietly pivoted its LPG and LNG imports toward the US. The strategic picture: reserves are thinner, Gulf flows remain offline, and the pressure on both Tehran and Washington to reach a Hormuz deal is mounting from every direction.
sources: Reuters, Times Now, CNBC-TV18, Telesur, AzerNews/GIE, Wood Mackenzie, IEA, US News/Reuters, Seeking Alpha, World Energy News, The Hindu BusinessLine, Moneycontrol, PTI, ET Now, Financial Times
